name: Gladstone's Land
description: Gladstone's Land is a surviving six-storey Old Town tenement on the Lawnmarket, its earliest recorded building dating to 1501. In 1617 the prosperous merchant Thomas Gledstanes and his wife Bessie Cunningham bought and rebuilt it, raising it to its present height and completing the work by 1620 with elaborate painted ceilings, later hidden under plaster and only rediscovered decades on. By the mid-1800s the Old Town's wealthier residents had long since decamped to the New Town, leaving the building to decline until the National Trust for Scotland rescued it from demolition in 1934, restoring it as a house museum reopened after a further £1.5 million refurbishment in 2021.
interesting_fact: The reconstructed timber-fronted shopfront on the ground floor recreates the arcaded booths once common along the medieval Royal Mile, almost all demolished elsewhere by later street widening. Above the door hangs a gilt-copper hawk with outstretched wings, a punning shop sign on the family name: 'gled' is the old Scots word for a kite or hawk. Past residents ranged from cloth merchants to an episcopalian minister of St Giles', and the museum still draws well over a quarter of a million visitors a year.

name: The Hub
description: This dark neo-Gothic building on the corner of Castlehill and Johnston Terrace was built in 1842-1845 as Victoria Hall, a joint design by Scottish architect James Gillespie Graham and the English Gothic Revival architect Augustus Pugin, meant to give the Church of Scotland's General Assembly a proper meeting hall. Queen Victoria laid its foundation stone in 1842. From 1929 it served as Highland Tolbooth St John's Church, holding services in both Gaelic and English, until its congregation united with Greyfriars Kirk in 1979 and the building closed, standing disused for over a decade. A five-year, £7.5 million conversion led by architect Benjamin Tindall - one of the most complex conservation projects ever undertaken in Scotland, involving more than 1,000 contributors - reopened it in 1999 as The Hub, home of the Edinburgh International Festival.
interesting_fact: At 71.7 metres, The Hub's spire is the tallest point in central Edinburgh, visible for miles across the city skyline. Queen Elizabeth II formally reopened the building in 1999, and despite its new life as a festival venue, cafe and box office, the Church of Scotland's General Assembly still returns to meet inside it every May, keeping alive the very purpose the hall was built for over 180 years ago.

name: Camera Obscura & World of Illusions
description: Edinburgh's camera obscura began life on Calton Hill in 1835, built by Maria Theresa Short around a telescope she inherited from her father, instrument-maker Thomas Short. When the city demolished her observatory there in 1851, she relocated the whole operation here to Castlehill, buying a townhouse and opening it in 1853 as Short's Observatory, Museum of Science and Art. After her death in 1869 her husband kept it running until 1892, when the pioneering town planner Patrick Geddes took over, renaming it the Outlook Tower and using its floors to display the world, Europe, Scotland and Edinburgh in ascending order, with the camera obscura crowning the summit.
interesting_fact: Category A listed since 1970, it claims to be the oldest purpose-built visitor attraction in Edinburgh and one of the oldest in Britain. The original camera obscura, a rotating mirror projecting a live moving image of the city onto a table below, still operates on the top floor exactly as it did in Short's day, now beneath five further floors of the World of Illusions' mirror mazes and vortex tunnels. Geddes later built a second Outlook Tower in Montpellier, France, since absorbed into the Scots College there.
source_notes: Maria Theresa Short/Short's Observatory origin story, the 1892 Patrick Geddes/Outlook Tower renaming, and the modern World of Illusions redevelopment corroborated via Wikipedia. name: The Witchery by the Castle
description: The Witchery occupies Boswell's Court, a merchant's townhouse built in 1595 for Thomas Lowthian and later named after the physician Dr John Boswell, whose family connections brought his relative James Boswell and Samuel Johnson to visit. By the 1970s the building had fallen into disrepair, serving latterly as Church of Scotland committee rooms, when 20-year-old chef James Thomson bought it in 1979, becoming Scotland's youngest licensee at a time when the Royal Mile was considered a poor location for a restaurant. In 1989 Thomson expanded into the former Castlehill School playground next door, creating the candlelit Secret Garden dining room, and later added nine Gothic-styled hotel suites above.
interesting_fact: The restaurant takes its name from the hundreds of men and women burned as witches on Castlehill during the 16th and 17th centuries, reputedly more than anywhere else in Scotland under James VI - a small bronze fountain, the Witches' Well, marks the spot just up the street. Local folklore holds The Witchery is itself haunted by one of the condemned, and its candlelit Gothic suites, one entered through a hidden bookcase door, have since hosted guests including Jack Nicholson and Andrew Lloyd Webber.

name: The Scotch Whisky Experience
description: Opened on 5 May 1988 as the Scotch Whisky Heritage Centre, this attraction occupies a former Victorian school building immediately beside the Castle esplanade. It was the brainchild of Alastair McIntosh, a managing director at whisky blender William Muir Ltd, who persuaded nineteen Scotch whisky companies to put up £2 million so visitors unable to reach the Highlands could still learn the spirit's history. The original tour carried guests through 300 years of whisky-making in mock oak barrels past thirteen theatrical sets, designed by Heritage Projects, the team behind York's Jorvik Viking Centre. A £3 million renovation in 2023 replaced the barrel ride with three new galleries: Origins, The Art of Whisky Making and Maturation.
interesting_fact: Since 2009 the centre has housed the Diageo Claive Vidiz Whisky Collection, 3,384 bottles gathered over 35 years by a single Brazilian enthusiast and unveiled by then First Minister Alex Salmond - it's certified by Guinness World Records as the largest Scotch whisky collection on Earth, and its oldest bottle, a Buchanan's blend, dates back to 1897. Downstairs, the Amber restaurant and whisky bar stocks more than 420 single malts, blends and liqueurs, and the attraction has now welcomed more than 8.5 million visitors since it first opened its doors in 1988.
source_notes: Founding date/founder, the original mock-barrel ride (designed by Heritage Projects, the Jorvik Viking Centre team), the 2009 Diageo Claive Vidiz Collection and the 2023 barrel-ride removal/renovation corroborated via Wikipedia. name: Tartan Weaving Mill
description: This building began as Castlehill Reservoir, built between 1849 and 1850 to supply the New Town with water, on a site that had earlier held a small 1755 reservoir and, before that, Christ Church chapel - demolished so its stone could help build the Tron Kirk. The huge cistern could hold two million gallons and discharge it at 5,000 gallons a minute; workmen digging the foundations reportedly found human remains and black oak coffins beneath the site. The reservoir was finally drained in 1992, opened briefly to public tours during the 1993 Doors Open Days, then bought and converted between 1995 and 1997 into the Old Town Weaving Company, later rebranded the Tartan Weaving Mill and Exhibition.
interesting_fact: Category B listed since 1987, the building still carries the Witches' Well, a small cast-iron fountain fixed to its outer wall commemorating those burned as witches nearby on Castlehill. Inside, a viewing window over the basement workshop lets visitors watch a working heritage loom weave tartan cloth in real time, a rare working link to the site's water-powered industrial past.

name: Cannonball House
description: Built in 1630 for furrier and skinner Alexander Mure and his wife Margaret Niellems - their initials and the date still carved above the door as 'AM MN 1630' - this Category A listed townhouse stands at the top of Castlehill, right by the entrance to the Castle esplanade. A 1913 restoration for the Edinburgh School Board converted it into an annex of the neighbouring Castlehill School, removing the narrow Blair's Close that had run through the building, though salvaged architectural fragments were reused elsewhere in the city. After the school closed in 1951 the building housed the Castlehill Urban Studies Centre and later a base for Edinburgh Festival walking tours, before becoming a restaurant under the Contini family in 2014.
interesting_fact: The house takes its name from the iron cannonball still lodged in its west-facing wall. Popular legend claims it was fired from the Castle's Half Moon Battery at Bonnie Prince Charlie during the 1745 Jacobite rising, but the more likely explanation is far less dramatic: engineers are thought to have fixed it there around 1675 to mark the exact gravitational height needed for Edinburgh's first piped water supply, drawn from springs at Comiston, to reach this point by gravity alone.
source_notes: 1630 construction for Alexander Mure/Margaret Niellems, the 1913 Castlehill School annex conversion and the two competing cannonball explanations (1745 Jacobite siege legend vs the more likely 1675 gravity-height water-supply marker) corroborated via Wikipedia. name: Ramsay Garden
description: Ramsay Garden takes its name from the poet and wigmaker Allan Ramsay the Elder, who built an octagonal house nicknamed 'Goosepie House' for its odd roofline here in 1733, later joined by a short Georgian terrace called Ramsay Street in 1760. Its present striking form dates from 1890-1893, when the pioneering town planner and biologist Patrick Geddes redeveloped the site as part of his wider campaign to regenerate Edinburgh's decaying Old Town, deliberately mixing university students, working artisans and wealthier residents in one community. Architect Stewart Henbest Capper designed the sixteen-apartment complex, with Sydney Mitchell completing construction after Capper's health failed. Today it remains private residential apartments and cannot be entered or accessed by visitors - it's best appreciated from the street outside, where its towers and balconies are clearly visible.
interesting_fact: Built in ornate Scots Baronial style, with red ashlar stonework beneath white harled upper storeys, towers and prominent balconies, Ramsay Garden is one of the most photographed silhouettes on the Edinburgh skyline, clearly visible from Princes Street far below. Geddes himself was fond enough of the result to call it 'the seven-towered castle I built for my beloved'. Past residents have included Ramsay's own descendants and the Royal Scottish Academy artist George Clark Stanton.
source_notes: Allan Ramsay's 1733 Goosepie House origin, Patrick Geddes' 1890-1893 redevelopment, architect Stewart Henbest Capper (completed by Sydney Mitchell) and the 'seven-towered castle' quote corroborated via Wikipedia. name: Castle Esplanade
description: The broad flat esplanade in front of Edinburgh Castle was created in 1753 as a military parade ground, built up using spoil excavated from the foundations of the Royal Exchange down on the High Street, then widened and given its present north wall and railings in 1816. Free to enter without a castle ticket, it offers sweeping views north to the Firth of Forth and south to the Pentland Hills. Since 1950 it has hosted the Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo every August - the first show had just eight items and drew 6,000 spectators, compared with the roughly 10,000-seat temporary stadium built and dismantled here each summer today.
interesting_fact: Statues of Robert the Bruce and William Wallace flank the Castle's gatehouse at the esplanade's western end, while scattered across its edges are a small bronze Witches' Well commemorating those executed for witchcraft nearby, commissioned by Patrick Geddes in 1894; a memorial to the 78th Highlanders topped by an elephant, remembering a regimental mascot said to have enjoyed the soldiers' beer; a statue of Prince Frederick, Duke of York, of nursery-rhyme fame; and the grave of dragoon Charles Ewart, who captured a French army standard at Waterloo in 1815.

name: Edinburgh Castle
description: Edinburgh Castle sits on Castle Rock, the plug of an extinct volcano that has made this one of the most defensible sites in Scotland since at least the Iron Age, when it held a hillfort roughly 3,000 years ago. It became a royal residence under King Malcolm III Canmore in the 11th century and went on to be besieged more often than almost any other fortress in Britain, including a celebrated night raid in 1314 - led by Thomas Randolph, Earl of Moray, nephew of Robert the Bruce - that recaptured it from English hands by scaling the crag under cover of darkness. Today it's a UNESCO World Heritage Site holding the Honours of Scotland (the country's crown jewels) and the Stone of Destiny, used for centuries in the coronation of Scottish monarchs.
interesting_fact: Tucked within the walls, St Margaret's Chapel is the oldest surviving building in Edinburgh, built around 1130 by King David I and named for his canonised mother; barely large enough for a handful of people, it is still used today for small weddings and christenings. Every day at 1pm (except Sundays, Good Friday and Christmas Day) a gun fires from Mills Mount Battery - a tradition begun in 1861 so ships out in the Forth could set their chronometers even when fog hid the Nelson Monument's time ball on Calton Hill.

name: The Witches' Well
description: Set into the wall at the foot of Castle Esplanade, this small cast-iron drinking fountain marks the site of Edinburgh's principal witch-burning ground. It was commissioned in 1894 by town planner Sir Patrick Geddes and designed by his friend John Duncan, a leading figure of the Scottish Celtic Revival, and fixed to the outer wall of the newly built Castlehill Reservoir - the same building that later became the neighbouring Tartan Weaving Mill. A plaque explaining its symbolism was added in 1912. Roman numerals worked into the bronze relief, 1479 and 1722, bracket the two and a half centuries during which Scotland's Witchcraft Act sent an estimated 300 people to their deaths on this spot alone.
interesting_fact: The relief pairs a serene face with a wicked one, both entwined by a serpent coiled around Hygieia, Greek goddess of health, and her father Asclepius, god of medicine - a reminder that the same knowledge could heal or condemn its holder. A sprig of foxglove beside them makes the same point twice over: it is both a heart medicine and a poison. Scotland executed an estimated 1,500 to 2,000 people for witchcraft between the 16th and 18th centuries, a rate of persecution proportionally far higher than the more famous Salem trials three thousand miles away.

name: The India Cross
description: This sandstone Celtic cross, raised on Castle Esplanade in 1862, commemorates 256 officers, non-commissioned officers and men of the 78th Highlanders - the Ross-shire Buffs - who died relieving the besieged British garrison at Lucknow during what an on-site Historic Environment Scotland panel now terms the Indian Rebellion or Mutiny of 1857-8. Indian soldiers had risen against British rule and besieged the city that June; when the 78th fought through the rebel lines to relieve it that September, the whole regiment was voted the Victoria Cross by ballot - a mechanism reserved for collective acts of gallantry too widespread to credit to one man - and the relieving commander General Henry Havelock is said to have declared he had 'never seen better conduct,' adding, 'I am not a Highlander but I wish I was one.'
interesting_fact: The regiment's elephant badge dates to the Battle of Assaye in 1803 and is carved into the cross itself. Around thirty years later the 78th brought a real elephant back to Edinburgh Castle - the animal reportedly led parades through the city, drank beer poured through the soldiers' canteen window, and was stabled alongside the regiment's horses. The 78th's lineage continues today within the Highlanders battalion of the Royal Regiment of Scotland.

name: Scottish Horse Memorial
description: This granite Celtic cross on Castle Esplanade was unveiled in 1904 to the men of the Scottish Horse, a yeomanry regiment raised in 1900 to fight in the Second Boer War. Two regiments were recruited that year from Scotland, Australia and South Africa to help Britain annex the South African Republic and Orange Free State, and the volunteers fought a brutal guerrilla campaign of night raids and farm-burning against Boer commandos. The design is credited to William Tait-Conner, with the granite carved by the firm Stewart McGlashan & Son; the regiment itself was disbanded at Edinburgh Castle in 1902, its lineage carried on today by the Scottish and North Irish Yeomanry.
interesting_fact: An identical memorial was unveiled the same year on Caledonia Hill in Kensington, Johannesburg, where it later became the official war memorial of the Transvaal Scottish regiment. Both crosses commemorate several Zulu scouts who served and died alongside the Scottish Horse - a rare instance of Black South African soldiers being formally named on a colonial-era war memorial - though sources disagree on the exact number honoured: Edinburgh's own on-site panel says three, while an account of the Johannesburg original says four.

name: The Afghan Needle
description: Known locally as the Afghan Needle, this pink Peterhead granite obelisk on Castle Esplanade was raised in 1882-83 by public subscription to the 105 officers, non-commissioned officers and men of the 72nd Duke of Albany's Own Highlanders who were killed in action or died of wounds and disease during the First and Second Anglo-Afghan Wars of 1839-42 and 1878-80. Standing 3.5 metres tall behind iron railings and designed by the Aberdeen firm MacDonald, Field & Company, its base carries every name, rank and regiment, grouped by how each man died. It is listed Grade II* by Historic Environment Scotland.
interesting_fact: The 72nd amalgamated with the 78th Highlanders - commemorated by this leg's own India Cross a few steps away - to form the Seaforth Highlanders in the army reforms of 1881, only a year or two before this memorial itself went up. Both regiments' lineage now continues together within the Highlanders battalion of the Royal Regiment of Scotland, so the esplanade's two 19th-century war memorials effectively honour the same modern regimental family.

name: The Gatehouse
description: The Gatehouse forming Edinburgh Castle's main entrance looks centuries old but is a Victorian addition, built in 1886-88 in Scots Baronial style to give the fortress a grander, more romantic approach befitting its status as a national monument - reportedly designed in some secrecy, since military authorities feared a cosmetic addition to a still-functioning garrison might draw public criticism. Flanking the archway in twin canopied niches, added decades later in 1929 to mark the 600th anniversary of Robert the Bruce's death, stand bronze statues of Bruce and William Wallace; the drawbridge and portcullis groove above the arch are both still in working order.
interesting_fact: Funded by a bequest from Captain Hugh Reid and erected by the Corporation of Edinburgh, the statues were unveiled on 28 May 1929: Bruce, by sculptor Thomas J. Clapperton, wears his crown and carries an axe and shield; Wallace, by Alexander Carrick, grips a claymore. Both stand in niches designed by the architect Sir Robert Lorimer, who had designed the castle's own Scottish National War Memorial just a couple of years earlier, in 1927.

name: Robert the Bruce Statue
description: Standing in a canopied niche to the left of Edinburgh Castle's Gatehouse, this bronze figure of Robert the Bruce was sculpted by Thomas J. Clapperton and unveiled on 28 May 1929, the 600th anniversary year of the king's death. Bruce is shown crowned and armoured, gripping a battleaxe in one hand and a heraldic shield in the other - the pose recalling his decisive personal combat with Sir Henry de Bohun on the eve of Bannockburn in 1314, when he split the English knight's skull with a single axe blow while mounted on a small palfrey rather than a war-horse. The statue, and its companion figure of William Wallace on the Gatehouse's other side, were funded by a bequest from Captain Hugh Reid and chosen through a public design competition that proved surprisingly divisive, sparking heated debate in the Scottish press throughout 1928 and 1929 over how the nation's two great medieval heroes should be portrayed.
interesting_fact: Bruce seized the Scottish throne in 1306, was excommunicated and hunted as a fugitive - the source of the famous, probably apocryphal, tale of a spider inspiring him to try again after defeat - before his victory at Bannockburn in 1314 secured Scotland's independence in fact if not yet in law. He died in 1329, reputedly of leprosy, and asked that his heart be carried on crusade after his death; it was eventually brought home and is buried at Melrose Abbey, while the rest of him lies at Dunfermline Abbey.

name: William Wallace Statue
description: Standing in a matching niche to the right of the Gatehouse archway, this bronze figure of William Wallace was sculpted by Alexander Carrick and unveiled alongside its Robert the Bruce counterpart on 28 May 1929. Wallace is shown in chainmail and a plaid, gripping a claymore, with a helmet resting at his feet - both statues share niches designed by the architect Sir Robert Lorimer and were funded by the same Hugh Reid bequest that paid for the Bruce figure opposite.
interesting_fact: Wallace led the rebel Scottish army to victory over a much larger English force at the Battle of Stirling Bridge in September 1297 and was appointed Guardian of Scotland, but was defeated the following year at Falkirk. Betrayed and captured in 1305, he was taken to London and executed as a traitor to a crown he had never sworn allegiance to - his death only hardening Scottish resistance that culminated in Bruce's victory at Bannockburn sixteen years later. Braveheart (1995) popularised his story worldwide but takes wide liberties with the history; the real Wallace, for instance, almost certainly never wore a kilt, which did not yet exist in his lifetime.

name: Ensign Ewart Memorial and Grave
description: Charles Ewart, a sergeant in the Royal North British Dragoons - the regiment later known as the Royal Scots Greys - captured the eagle standard of the French 45th Regiment in brutal hand-to-hand combat at the Battle of Waterloo on 18 June 1815, fighting off a standard-bearer, a lancer and an infantryman in quick succession before carrying the eagle clear of the fighting. He was promoted to Ensign in reward and became a minor celebrity in Scotland, reportedly acquainted with Sir Walter Scott, though by his own account he shunned the attention. Ewart died in 1846 near Manchester and was buried in Salford, where his grave was later paved over and forgotten.
interesting_fact: His remains were rediscovered in the 1930s and reburied here on the Castle Esplanade, with a granite memorial unveiled at an official ceremony on 16 April 1938, attended by a guard of honour and the regimental band of the Royal Scots Greys. His own account of the fight survives almost word for word: 'I took the eagle from the enemy... he made a thrust at my groin; I parried it off and cut him down through the head.' In his memory, the Royal Scots Greys - and the Royal Scots Dragoon Guards that succeeded them - still wear an eagle badge today.
